concepts.title: OSI vs TCP/IP Encapsulation and PDU Overhead
concepts.content: Network stacks encapsulate payloads by prepending headers at each layer: Application data becomes L4 segments/datagrams, L3 packets, and L2 frames. Standard Ethernet (1500-byte MTU) with IPv4 (20B) and TCP (20B) leaves 1460 bytes for payload (97.3% efficiency). Adding VXLAN (50B overhead) shrinks inner MTU to 1450B; inspect interface MTU with `ip -d link show`.
concepts.image_prompt: Stacked horizontal block diagram showing Ethernet Header 14B, IPv4 Header 20B, TCP Header 20B, Payload 1460B, and FCS 4B with bracket arrows indicating L2 Frame, L3 Packet, and L4 Segment boundaries.

concepts.title: Ethernet L2 Switching, MAC Learning, and VLAN Tagging (802.1Q)
concepts.content: Switches populate Content Addressable Memory (CAM) tables by mapping source MAC addresses to ingress ports and flood unknown unicast or broadcast (`ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`) frames. IEEE 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag after the source MAC containing a 12-bit VLAN ID (up to 4094 VLANs). Inspect Linux bridge forwarding entries with `bridge fdb show`.
concepts.image_prompt: Packet header diagram inserting a 4-byte 802.1Q Tag containing TPID 0x8100 and 12-bit VID between Source MAC and EtherType, connected to a Switch CAM Table mapping MAC to Port and VLAN.

concepts.title: ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP)
concepts.content: ARP resolves IPv4 addresses to L2 MACs via broadcast requests, creating L2 broadcast storms at scale and risking ARP spoofing. IPv6 replaces ARP with ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation (Type 135) and Neighbor Advertisement (Type 136) using solicited-node multicast (`ff02::1:ff00:0/104`). View kernel neighbor cache states (`REACHABLE`, `STALE`, `DELAY`) using `ip neigh show`.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram comparing IPv4 ARP Broadcast Request to all hosts versus IPv6 ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation to Solicited-Node Multicast group ff02::1:ffXX:XXXX with Unicast Neighbor Advertisement reply.

concepts.title: IPv4 CIDR Subnetting and Longest Prefix Match (LPM)
concepts.content: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) aggregates IP ranges using variable-length prefix masks. Routers forward packets using Longest Prefix Match (LPM), always selecting the route with the highest prefix length (e.g., `/26` beats `/24`) before evaluating administrative distance or metric. Test exact kernel route selection and source IP binding with `ip route get 10.20.30.40`.
concepts.image_prompt: Routing trie diagram showing incoming packet 10.1.2.15 matching three prefixes 10.0.0.0/8, 10.1.0.0/16, and 10.1.2.0/24, with decision arrow selecting 10.1.2.0/24 as Longest Prefix Match.

concepts.title: IPv6 Addressing, SLAAC, and Dual-Stack Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305)
concepts.content: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, eliminating NAT and supporting Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) via Router Advertisements (`fe80::/10` link-local). Dual-stack clients avoid broken IPv6 blackholes using RFC 8305 Happy Eyeballs: querying `AAAA` and `A` records concurrently and starting a TCP connection fallback timer (typically 250ms) if IPv6 stalls. Verify IPv6 paths with `ping -6`.
concepts.image_prompt: Timeline flow diagram showing Client sending parallel DNS AAAA and A queries, initiating IPv6 SYN first, starting a 250ms Happy Eyeballs timer, and launching fallback IPv4 SYN in parallel.

concepts.title: MTU, MSS Clamping, and Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD)
concepts.content: When an IPv4 packet with the Don't Fragment (`DF`) bit exceeds a link's MTU, the router drops it and returns ICMP Type 3 Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed). Misconfigured firewalls blocking ICMP cause silent PMTUD blackholes where handshakes succeed but bulk transfers stall. Mitigate via TCP MSS clamping (`iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu`).
concepts.image_prompt: Network topology diagram showing Sender (MTU 1500) -> Router -> Tunnel (MTU 1400) -> Receiver, with Router returning ICMP Type 3 Code 4 packet to Sender and Firewall blocking it.

concepts.title: NAT, SNAT/DNAT, and Linux Conntrack Exhaustion
concepts.content: Stateful NAT rewrites source (SNAT/Masquerade) or destination (DNAT) IP/port tuples and tracks flows in the kernel `nf_conntrack` table. High-rate short-lived connections or SYN floods can fill the table (`nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet`), dropping all new traffic. Monitor usage against `net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max` using `sysctl net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_count` and bypass tracking for stateless flows with `nft notrack`.
concepts.image_prompt: Flow diagram showing Packet entering PREROUTING DNAT, consulting nf_conntrack State Table, routing to POSTROUTING SNAT, with an overflow gauge on the State Table labeled nf_conntrack_max Drop.

concepts.title: BGP Peering, AS-PATH, and Anycast Traffic Engineering
concepts.content: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP-4, TCP port 179) exchanges reachability between Autonomous Systems (AS). Route selection evaluates Weight, Local Preference (outbound traffic control), shortest `AS_PATH` (inbound control via prepending), Origin, and MED. Anycast advertises identical IP prefixes from multiple geographic PoPs so ingress routers direct users to the topologically nearest instance. Inspect FRR state via `vtysh -c 'show bgp summary'`.
concepts.image_prompt: Topology diagram showing Client ASN 65001 connected to two Anycast PoPs advertising 198.51.100.0/24 via ASN 65010 (AS_PATH length 1) and ASN 65020 (AS_PATH prepended length 3), routing to shortest path.

concepts.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake, SYN Cookies, and Listen Backlog Queues
concepts.content: TCP connections establish via `SYN`, `SYN-ACK`, and `ACK`, moving sockets through the kernel SYN queue (`net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog`) into the accept queue (`net.core.somaxconn`). If the application stalls `accept()`, the accept queue overflows (`ListenOverflows` in `nstat -az`). Enable `net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1` to encode state cryptographically in sequence numbers when the SYN queue fills.
concepts.image_prompt: Two-stage queue diagram showing Client SYN entering Kernel SYN Queue, returning SYN-ACK, Client ACK moving socket to Accept Queue limited by somaxconn, and Application calling accept().

concepts.title: TCP Connection Teardown, TIME_WAIT, and Ephemeral Port Exhaustion
concepts.content: Active closers transition through `FIN_WAIT_1`, `FIN_WAIT_2`, and enter `TIME_WAIT` for `2 * MSL` (60s on Linux) to absorb delayed packets and ensure remote `LAST_ACK` receipt. Reverse proxies opening thousands of outbound connections per second to a single backend IP can exhaust the ephemeral port range (`net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range`). Enable `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1` to safely reuse `TIME_WAIT` sockets when TCP timestamps are active.
concepts.image_prompt: State transition diagram between Active Closer and Passive Closer showing FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK exchange, Active Closer entering 60s TIME_WAIT state, and Ephemeral Port Pool depletion arrow.

concepts.title: TCP Flow Control, Sliding Window, and Window Scaling (RFC 7323)
concepts.content: TCP flow control prevents a fast sender from overwhelming a slow receiver's socket buffer (`SO_RCVBUF`) by advertising the available Receive Window (`rwnd`) in every ACK header. Because the original 16-bit field caps `rwnd` at 65,535 bytes, RFC 7323 adds a Window Scale option during the `SYN` handshake (shift count up to 14, allowing 1 GiB windows). Check `net.ipv4.tcp_window_scaling=1`.
concepts.image_prompt: Sliding window byte-stream diagram showing Sent and ACKed, Sent Not ACKed, Usable Window, and Outside Window sections bounded by Receive Window rwnd multiplied by 2^ScaleFactor.

concepts.title: Bandwidth-Delay Product (BDP) and Socket Buffer Tuning
concepts.content: The Bandwidth-Delay Product (`BDP = Bandwidth * RTT`) defines the volume of unacknowledged in-flight data required to saturate a link. A 10 Gbps link with 20 ms RTT requires `10e9 / 8 * 0.02 = 25 MB` of buffer capacity; standard 4 MB max buffers cap throughput below 1.6 Gbps. Tune `net.ipv4.tcp_rmem` and `net.ipv4.tcp_wmem` (`min default max` in bytes) to exceed peak BDP.
concepts.image_prompt: Pipe capacity diagram showing Bandwidth as pipe height and RTT as pipe length, labeled Volume = Bandwidth x RTT = 25 MB, compared against an undersized 4 MB Socket Buffer capping throughput.

concepts.title: TCP Congestion Control: CUBIC vs BBR
concepts.content: CUBIC is a loss-based algorithm that grows the congestion window (`cwnd`) via a cubic function of time since the last loss event, which tends to fill deep router buffers (bufferbloat) before dropping packets. Google's BBR is model-based, probing bottleneck bandwidth (`BtlBw`) and minimum RTT (`RTprop`) to pace packets near optimal operating points even with shallow buffers or random loss. Enable via `sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr`.
concepts.image_prompt: Dual line chart of Congestion Window and RTT over time comparing CUBIC sawtooth growth into bufferbloat queue buildup versus BBR steady pacing at BtlBw and RTprop operating point.

concepts.title: Nagle's Algorithm (TCP_NODELAY) vs Delayed ACKs Interaction
concepts.content: Nagle's algorithm buffers small writes until in-flight data is acknowledged or a full MSS accumulates, while Delayed ACKs wait up to 40–200 ms before sending an empty ACK hoping to piggyback on a response. When an RPC client sends a multi-write request without receiving an immediate reply, both ends deadlock until the Delayed ACK timer expires, adding 40 ms latency spikes. Always set `TCP_NODELAY` on RPC sockets.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram showing Client sending Write 1, buffering Write 2 due to Nagle waiting for ACK, while Server holds ACK for 40ms Delayed ACK timer waiting for application response.

concepts.title: UDP Mechanics, Socket Buffer Drops, and QUIC (RFC 9000)
concepts.content: UDP adds only an 8-byte header (ports, length, checksum) with no handshake, retransmission, or head-of-line blocking, making it ideal for DNS, telemetry, and QUIC. If an application reads slower than packets arrive, the kernel drops datagrams at the receive buffer (`RcvbufErrors` in `nstat -az` or `ss -u -a -m`). QUIC layers TLS 1.3 encryption, independent stream multiplexing, and connection migration via Connection IDs atop UDP.
concepts.image_prompt: Side-by-side protocol stack comparing TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 suffering single-stream packet loss blocking all streams versus UDP+QUIC+HTTP/3 isolating packet loss to Stream 2 while Stream 1 and 3 continue.

concepts.title: Linux Epoll (`EPOLLET` vs `EPOLLLT`) and `SO_REUSEPORT`
concepts.content: High-concurrency RPC servers use `epoll_wait()` for $O(1)$ readiness notifications per active event. Level-triggered (`EPOLLLT`, default) re-notifies until the buffer empties; Edge-triggered (`EPOLLET`) notifies only on state transitions, requiring non-blocking sockets (`O_NONBLOCK`) read in a loop until `EAGAIN` to avoid stalled requests. Combine with `SO_REUSEPORT` so the kernel hashes incoming connections across per-core worker threads without accept-lock contention.
concepts.image_prompt: Architecture diagram showing NIC RX Queues hashing flows via SO_REUSEPORT to separate Worker Threads, each running its own non-blocking epoll_wait loop reading sockets until EAGAIN.

concepts.title: DNS Resolution Hierarchy, EDNS0, and Negative Caching (RFC 2308)
concepts.content: Stub resolvers read `/etc/resolv.conf` and query recursive resolvers, which traverse Root (`.`), TLD, and Authoritative nameservers. Standard UDP DNS caps at 512 bytes; EDNS0 (OPT pseudo-record) negotiates larger UDP payloads (typically 1232 bytes to avoid IPv6 fragmentation) before falling back to TCP. Remember that `NXDOMAIN` responses are cached for the SOA record's minimum TTL (RFC 2308), so premature checks before DNS cutovers can cache failures; inspect with `dig +trace +dnssec`.
concepts.image_prompt: Flow diagram showing Stub Resolver -> Recursive Resolver -> Root -> TLD -> Authoritative Server, highlighting EDNS0 1232B UDP payload negotiation and SOA Minimum TTL Negative Cache storage.

concepts.title: Kubernetes DNS `ndots:5` Amplification and NodeLocal DNSCache
concepts.content: Kubernetes pods default to `options ndots:5` in `/etc/resolv.conf` with 3 search domains (`<ns>.svc.cluster.local`, `svc.cluster.local`, `cluster.local`). Any external hostname with fewer than 5 dots (e.g., `api.stripe.com`) triggers 3 sequential `A` and 3 `AAAA` search-path queries (6 extra queries) before querying the absolute FQDN, exhausting CoreDNS conntrack entries. Append a trailing dot (`api.stripe.com.`), lower `ndots:2`, or deploy NodeLocal DNSCache on `169.254.20.10`.
concepts.image_prompt: Decision flowchart showing Pod looking up api.stripe.com (2 dots < ndots:5), looping through 3 cluster search domains returning NXDOMAIN 6 times before resolving absolute FQDN.

concepts.title: TLS 1.3 Handshake (1-RTT / 0-RTT), ALPN, and Replay Risks
concepts.content: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removes legacy RSA key transport and completes negotiation in 1-RTT by sending `key_share` extensions inside `ClientHello`. Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN) selects `h2` (gRPC/HTTP/2) or `http/1.1` within the same flight, saving an extra round trip. While 0-RTT session resumption sends application data on the first packet, it lacks forward secrecy for early data and is vulnerable to replay attacks—never enable 0-RTT for non-idempotent RPCs. Verify with `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1_3 -alpn h2`.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram comparing TLS 1.2 (2-RTT handshake before Application Data) against TLS 1.3 (1-RTT ClientHello with key_share and ALPN h2 followed by ServerHello and encrypted data).

concepts.title: Mutual TLS (mTLS), X.509 SAN Validation, and SPIFFE IDs
concepts.content: In Mutual TLS (mTLS), the server sends a `CertificateRequest` during the TLS handshake, requiring the client to present an X.509 certificate and prove possession of the private key via `CertificateVerify`. Modern TLS libraries ignore the deprecated Common Name (`CN`) and strictly validate Subject Alternative Names (`SAN` DNS or URI fields). Zero-trust service meshes encode workload identity as a SPIFFE URI SAN (e.g., `spiffe://prod.cluster.local/ns/payments/sa/checkout`) with short-lived (1–24h) auto-rotated certs.
concepts.image_prompt: Handshake diagram showing Server sending CertificateRequest and Client returning X.509 Certificate + CertificateVerify signature, with callout box zooming into X.509 v3 Subject Alternative Name URI spiffe://domain/ns/sa.

concepts.title: HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive vs HTTP/2 Binary Framing and HPACK
concepts.content: HTTP/1.1 serializes requests per TCP connection; even with pipelining, a slow response causes Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking, forcing clients to open 6+ parallel TCP connections. HTTP/2 multiplexes concurrent bidirectional streams over a single TCP connection by splitting messages into interleaved binary `HEADERS` and `DATA` frames tagged with a 31-bit Stream ID, and compresses repetitive headers using HPACK static/dynamic tables. Note that a single lost TCP segment still stalls all HTTP/2 streams at the kernel layer.
concepts.image_prompt: Comparison diagram showing HTTP/1.1 using 3 separate TCP connections with sequential blocked requests versus HTTP/2 multiplexing interleaved Stream 1 and Stream 3 HEADERS and DATA frames over 1 TCP connection.

concepts.title: L4 vs L7 Load Balancing and Maglev Consistent Hashing
concepts.content: L4 load balancers (IPVS, AWS NLB, Cilium) forward TCP/UDP packets or flows by hashing the 5-tuple (`src_ip, dst_ip, src_port, dst_port, proto`) without terminating TLS or parsing application framing. L7 proxies (Envoy, NGINX, ALB) terminate TLS, inspect HTTP/2 frames, and route per-request. To prevent backend pool changes from reshuffling all active L4 flows and resetting stateful connections, Maglev uses a 65,537-slot permutation lookup table providing minimal disruption consistent hashing.
concepts.image_prompt: Split architecture diagram showing L4 Load Balancer hashing 5-tuple via Maglev Permutation Table directly to Backend TCP sockets versus L7 Proxy terminating TLS and routing individual HTTP/2 streams to different backends.

concepts.title: The gRPC Long-Lived HTTP/2 Load Balancing Pitfall
concepts.content: Because gRPC multiplexes all RPC calls over a single persistent HTTP/2 TCP connection, placing a standard L4 load balancer (or Kubernetes ClusterIP `Service`) in front of gRPC backends pins all traffic from a client pod to one backend pod for the connection's lifetime, rendering new replicas idle. Fix this by using an L7 proxy (Envoy/Linkerd), configuring server `MaxConnectionAge` to force periodic reconnects, or using client-side `round_robin` balancing with headless DNS (`clusterIP: None`).
concepts.image_prompt: Diagram showing left side (Broken L4): Client sending 100 RPCs over 1 HTTP/2 connection pinned via ClusterIP to Pod A while Pod B and C sit at 0% CPU; right side (Fixed L7/Client-Side): RPCs distributed evenly across Pods A, B, and C.

concepts.title: RPC Fundamentals: Stubs, Marshaling, and the Fallacies of Distributed Computing
concepts.content: Remote Procedure Calls (RPC) make inter-process network communication resemble local function invocation: a generated client stub marshals parameters into a wire format, transmits them via a transport runtime, and unmarshals the server skeleton's reply. Treating RPCs as local calls leads to cascading outages because networks violate local assumptions: latency is non-zero, bandwidth is finite, packets drop, and partial failures occur where the caller cannot tell if a timed-out request executed on the server.
concepts.image_prompt: Layered flow diagram showing Caller -> Client Stub (Marshal) -> Network Transport (with packet loss/latency hazard icon) -> Server Skeleton (Unmarshal) -> Callee Implementation.

concepts.title: Protocol Buffers Wire Encoding: Tag-Length-Value, Varints, and ZigZag
concepts.content: Protobuf encodes messages as compact binary Tag-Length-Value (TLV) streams without field names. Each field prefix stores a varint key `(field_number << 3) | wire_type`, meaning field numbers `1–15` fit in a single byte—reserve them for hot fields. Standard `int32`/`int64` varints use 10 bytes for negative numbers because the sign bit is set; always use `sint32`/`sint64` for signed values, which apply ZigZag encoding (`(n << 1) ^ (n >> 31)`) to map small negative integers to small unsigned varints.
concepts.image_prompt: Bit-level byte layout diagram showing Tag byte split into 5-bit Field Number and 3-bit Wire Type, followed by Varint MSB continuation bits and ZigZag mapping table (-1 -> 1, 1 -> 2, -2 -> 3).

concepts.title: Protobuf Schema Evolution: `reserved` Fields and Wire Compatibility
concepts.content: Backward and forward compatibility in Protobuf relies solely on field numbers and wire types, never field names. Never reuse a deleted field number or change a field's incompatible wire type (e.g., `int32` to `string`), as older binaries will silently corrupt or misparse payloads. Always block retired identifiers and names in your `.proto` schema using `reserved 4, 15, 9 to 11; reserved "old_field";` and verify compatibility in CI with `buf breaking --against .git#branch=main`.
concepts.image_prompt: Schema comparison diagram showing v1.proto (field 4 = string name) and v2.proto with two branches: Unsafe Reuse (field 4 = int32 id causing parse corruption) vs Safe Evolution (reserved 4; field 5 = int32 id).

concepts.title: JSON-RPC 2.0, Apache Thrift, and FlatBuffers / Cap'n Proto Trade-offs
concepts.content: Serialization choice trades human readability against CPU/allocation overhead. JSON-RPC 2.0 is text-based and easy to debug in browsers (`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"sum","params":[1,2],"id":1}`), but incurs high parsing CPU and payload size. Protobuf and Apache Thrift require an explicit deserialization allocation step into language objects, yielding compact payloads (~3–10x smaller than JSON). FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto use aligned offset tables for zero-copy reads directly from the mmap/socket buffer, ideal for sub-microsecond IPC or gaming.
concepts.image_prompt: 2x2 comparison matrix and pipeline diagram contrasting JSON (Text Parse -> Heap Objects), Protobuf/Thrift (Binary Decode -> Heap Objects), and FlatBuffers/Cap'n Proto (Aligned Binary Buffer -> Direct Zero-Copy Pointer Read).

concepts.title: gRPC 4 Streaming Modes and HTTP/2 Frame Mapping
concepts.content: gRPC supports four invocation patterns over a single HTTP/2 stream: Unary (`1 req -> 1 resp`), Server Streaming (`1 req -> N resp`), Client Streaming (`N req -> 1 resp`), and Bidirectional Streaming (`N <-> M` independent async messages). On the wire, a call starts with an HTTP/2 `HEADERS` frame carrying `:path: /pkg.Service/Method`, followed by length-prefixed Protobuf messages (1-byte compression flag + 4-byte big-endian length) inside `DATA` frames, and concludes with a trailing `HEADERS` frame carrying `grpc-status`.
concepts.image_prompt: HTTP/2 stream timeline showing initial HEADERS frame (:path, content-type), multiple DATA frames each containing 1B Compressed-Flag + 4B Message-Length + Protobuf Bytes, and final Trailers HEADERS frame (grpc-status: 0, END_STREAM).

concepts.title: gRPC Flow Control, `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE`, and Backpressure
concepts.content: In gRPC streaming, writing messages faster than the peer reads causes memory bloat unless bounded by HTTP/2 flow control (`WINDOW_UPDATE` frames at both stream and connection levels, default 65,535 bytes). In Go/Java/C++, inspect stream readiness or await the send buffer before producing the next message so HTTP/2 window exhaustion blocks the sender cleanly. For high-BDP WAN links, raise `InitialWindowSize` and `InitialConnWindowSize` (e.g., to `4–16 MiB`) or activates dynamic BDP probing.
concepts.image_prompt: Producer-Consumer pipeline showing Producer checking Stream IsReady/FlowControl Window before pushing to Send Buffer, connected across HTTP/2 link to Receiver returning WINDOW_UPDATE frames as application consumes messages.

concepts.title: gRPC Keepalive Ping (`PING` Frames) and `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM` (`GOAWAY`)
concepts.content: Intermediate NAT gateways and L4 load balancers silently drop idle TCP connections after 60–350 seconds without sending `RST` or `FIN`. gRPC detects dead channels by sending periodic HTTP/2 `PING` frames (`keepalive_time_ms`). However, if clients ping too aggressively (e.g., every 5s) without active streams when the server defaults to a 5-minute minimum (`GRPC_ARG_HTTP2_MIN_RECV_PING_INTERVAL_WITHOUT_DATA_MS`), the server terminates the connection with an HTTP/2 `GOAWAY` frame carrying error code `ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`. Always align client and server keepalive policies.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence diagram showing Client sending frequent HTTP/2 PING frames across NAT Firewall to Server, Server Ping Strike Counter exceeding threshold, and Server returning GOAWAY (ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM) closing connection.

concepts.title: gRPC Deadlines, `grpc-timeout` Header, and Context Cancellation Propagation
concepts.content: Every production RPC must set an absolute deadline (`WithTimeout` / `WithDeadline`); un-deadlined calls leak goroutines, file descriptors, and DB connections during downstream brownouts. gRPC serializes the remaining budget on the wire via the `grpc-timeout` HTTP/2 header (e.g., `500m` for 500 milliseconds). When Service A calls Service B which calls Service C, propagating the incoming `context.Context` automatically deducts local processing time from the downstream `grpc-timeout` and sends an HTTP/2 `RST_STREAM (CANCEL)` frame if the caller aborts.
concepts.image_prompt: Call chain diagram showing Client (1000ms budget) -> Service A (spends 200ms, sends grpc-timeout: 800m) -> Service B (spends 300ms, sends grpc-timeout: 500m) -> Service C, with reverse RST_STREAM (CANCEL) propagation arrow on timeout.

concepts.title: gRPC Status Codes vs HTTP Status Codes and Rich Error Details
concepts.content: Unlike REST APIs that overload HTTP status codes, gRPC always returns HTTP `200 OK` at the transport layer if the request reaches the gRPC server, placing the actual outcome in the HTTP/2 trailer `grpc-status` (`0 OK`, `3 INVALID_ARGUMENT`, `4 DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, `8 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`, `14 UNAVAILABLE`). Only load balancer/proxy failures produce non-200 HTTP codes (mapped to `UNAVAILABLE` or `INTERNAL`). Attach structured, typed error payloads using `google.rpc.Status` (`grpc-status-details-bin` trailer) rather than parsing error strings.
concepts.image_prompt: HTTP/2 response structure showing initial HEADERS (:status 200) -> DATA frames -> Trailing HEADERS containing grpc-status: 3, grpc-message, and base64-encoded grpc-status-details-bin unpacking into google.rpc.BadRequest.

concepts.title: Retries, Hedging, Exponential Backoff with Jitter, and Retry Storms
concepts.content: Retrying failed RPCs immediately or across multiple layers multiplies load (`N_layers^Retries`), turning a brief blip into a self-inflicted retry storm that prevents recovery. Restrict retries to transient status codes (`UNAVAILABLE`) on idempotent methods, use exponential backoff with full jitter (`sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))`), and enforce a client-side retry token bucket (e.g., max 10% retry overhead in gRPC service config `retryThrottling`). Use hedged requests only for read-only tail-latency reduction.
concepts.image_prompt: Two-panel diagram: left showing synchronized un-jittered retries causing traffic spikes across 3 service tiers (8x amplification); right showing Full Jitter spread plus Retry Token Bucket blocking retries when bucket drains below 50%.

concepts.title: Idempotency Keys and At-Least-Once RPC Execution
concepts.content: Because a network timeout after the request leaves the client leaves the outcome ambiguous (`DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` or `UNAVAILABLE`), safe retries provide at-least-once delivery and require server-side idempotency for state-mutating RPCs. Clients generate a UUIDv4/UUIDv7 `idempotency_key` per logical operation and pass it in the request proto. The server atomically inserts the key and response payload into a transactional outbox/deduplication table within the same database transaction, returning the cached response on duplicate retries.
concepts.image_prompt: Sequence and database transaction diagram showing Client retrying MutateRPC(idempotency_key=UUID-1), Server executing BEGIN TX -> INSERT key ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING -> returning cached committed result without double-charging.

concepts.title: Tail Latency Amplification (Fan-Out) and Circuit Breaking / Load Shedding
concepts.content: In a fan-out architecture where one ingress request queries 50 leaf RPC services in parallel, even if each leaf has a 99th percentile latency of 10 ms ($p=0.01$), the probability that at least one leaf exceeds 10 ms is $1 - (0.99)^{50} = 39.5\%$. Protect overloaded leaf nodes via server-side load shedding (CoDel queueing or concurrency limits like Envoy adaptive concurrency returning `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`) and client-side outlier detection (`consecutive_5xx` ejection) to avoid waiting on degraded pods.
concepts.image_prompt: Fan-out diagram showing Root Aggregator calling 50 Leaf Nodes in parallel where 1 slow node delays the entire response (39.5% probability), paired with an Envoy Circuit Breaker ejecting the unhealthy leaf node.

concepts.title: gRPC Reflection, Health Checking Protocol (`grpc.health.v1`), and `grpcurl`
concepts.content: Because Protobuf is not self-describing on the wire, enable the gRPC Server Reflection service (`grpc.reflection.v1.ServerReflection`) in non-public environments so CLI tools can dynamically fetch descriptors without local `.proto` files. Implement the standard `grpc.health.v1.Health/Check` and `Watch` RPCs so Kubernetes (`grpc:` liveness/readiness probes since v1.24) and L7 proxies can query per-service health (`SERVING`, `NOT_SERVING`). Debug live endpoints via `grpcurl -plaintext localhost:50051 list` and `grpcurl -d '{"id":1}' localhost:50051 pkg.Svc/Get`.
concepts.image_prompt: Interaction diagram showing grpcurl querying ServerReflection to fetch FileDescriptorProto then invoking pkg.Svc/Get, alongside Kubelet Probe calling grpc.health.v1.Health/Check receiving SERVING status.

concepts.title: ConnectRPC and gRPC-Web for Browser-to-Backend RPC
concepts.content: Web browsers (`fetch` / `XMLHttpRequest`) do not expose raw HTTP/2 frame control or HTTP/2 trailers, preventing native gRPC wire calls directly from browser JS. `gRPC-Web` works around this by encoding the trailing `grpc-status` inside the final length-prefixed body frame (`0x80` MSB flag) and typically requires an Envoy translation filter. `ConnectRPC` natively supports three protocols on the same server port: standard gRPC, gRPC-Web, and idiomatic HTTP POST/GET JSON inspectable directly in browser DevTools.
concepts.image_prompt: Tri-path architecture diagram showing Browser Client sending Connect/gRPC-Web (trailers in 0x80 body frame or JSON POST) and Backend Service sending standard HTTP/2 gRPC (trailers in HEADERS frame) to a single ConnectRPC Server.

concepts.title: Service Mesh Data Plane Architecture: Sidecar (`iptables` vs eBPF) vs Ambient
concepts.content: Traditional service meshes (Istio/Linkerd) inject an Envoy/Linkerd2-proxy sidecar container into every pod, using `iptables` `PREROUTING`/`OUTPUT` redirect rules (`15006`/`15001`) to intercept TCP traffic—adding 2 extra localhost TCP traversals per hop. eBPF socket redirection (`sockops`/`sk_msg`) bypasses the TCP/IP stack between application and local proxy sockets. Ambient mesh architectures replace per-pod sidecars with a per-node L4 `ztunnel` (handling mTLS/SPIFFE over HBONE HTTP/2 CONNECT tunnels) and optional L7 waypoint proxies.

concepts.title: W3C Trace Context Propagation (`traceparent`) Across RPC Boundaries
concepts.content: Distributed tracing links RPC hops into a single causal DAG by propagating context metadata in every outbound request header (`grpc-metadata`). The W3C Trace Context standard replaces proprietary headers with `traceparent: 00-<32-hex-trace-id>-<16-hex-parent-span-id>-<2-hex-flags>` (where flag `01` means sampled) and `tracestate` for vendor key-values. OpenTelemetry interceptors (`otelgrpc`) extract incoming `traceparent` metadata into `context.Context`, create a child span with a new `span-id` sharing the same `trace-id`, and inject it into downstream RPC calls.

concepts.title: Packet Capture and Debugging Encrypted gRPC Traffic (`tcpdump`, `ss`, `SSLKEYLOGFILE`)
concepts.content: When debugging production RPC hangs or resets, start with `ss -ti dst 10.0.1.5` to inspect live kernel TCP variables (`cwnd`, `rtt`, `retrans`, `unacked`) without packet capture overhead. To capture wire frames, run `tcpdump -nn -i any -s 0 -w rpc.pcap 'tcp port 50051'`. Because TLS 1.3 encrypts ALPN, HTTP/2 headers, and `DATA` frames, export `SSLKEYLOGFILE=/tmp/tls.keys` in a staging client or use eBPF (`ecapture`) so Wireshark can decrypt HTTP/2 streams and decode Protobuf payloads.
